verses.translation_literal: Oh the blessednesses of the man who has not walked in the counsel of wicked ones, and in the way of sinners has not stood, and in the seat of mockers has not sat.
verses.translation_dramatic: Blessed — oh, how blessed — is the one who will not walk where the wicked deal out their counsel, who will not plant his feet on the road the sinners keep, who will not settle himself in the seat where mockers sit and sneer.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalter opens not with a prayer or a hymn but with a happy-saying, and the word is plural: ’ashrê is a heap of blessings, "the happinesses of the man". Radak and Meiri both stress that it is only ever found in the plural. It is the voice of a wisdom teacher congratulating the listener on a way of life, the same cadence as the opening of Proverbs. Play it as a benediction said over a person, not a command.

The verse is built as three paired steps: walk (halakh), stand (‘amad), sit (yashav), set against counsel (‘etsah), way (derekh), seat (moshav), and three kinds of company: the wicked (resha‘im), sinners (hatta’im), mockers (letsim). The rabbis (Avodah Zarah 18b, quoted by Radak) read this as a slide: whoever walks with them will stop with them, and then sit among them. Ibn Ezra notes the older view that sitting is the worst, and Meiri raises the reverse reading, that walking is the deepest commitment. Keep the three verbs distinct for the actors; each is a posture.

The KJV makes the wicked "the ungodly", a religious label the Hebrew does not use: רָשָׁע means "guilty, in the wrong", a courtroom word, and "ungodly" imports a theological reading. KJV "scornful" for לֵצִים is archaic; the root means to speak with mocking eloquence (Metzudat Zion ties it to מליצה, "a polished phrase"), so these are cynics with a sharp tongue. KJV also turns the perfect verbs into a present "walketh not", flattening the settled, habitual character of the man; the Hebrew says he "has not walked", as a record of his life.

Who sits in the seat of the mockers? Radak, Meiri and Malbim agree: idle men who sit at street corners, filling their hours with gossip and ridicule, doing neither good nor harm but chasing wind. Meiri adds that they pass their time "in the sitting of corners" speaking of other people's affairs. Play the seat as a bench on the corner, not a bench of judges. (A moshav can also be a place where elders or councils sit, and one could hear a mocking assembly here; that is my own reading, not the commentators'.)

philological_notes.note: Plural construct of 'esher, 'happiness, good fortune'. Only occurs in plural, which both Radak and Meiri explain as blessing in many goods at once. It congratulates rather than prays. KJV 'Blessed' merges it with בָּרוּךְ (barukh), which is a blessing conferred by God.

Radak ties the root to restlessness and greed (Job 34:29, 'who can make trouble?'); Malbim says resha'im sin deliberately and with counsel, which is why the verse says 'counsel' of the wicked. In law the word is the opposite of 'in the right' (own reading). 'Ungodly' (KJV) is a theological gloss.

Mockers, scoffers: a speaker who ridicules with clever language. Metzudat Zion links it to melitsah, a polished saying; Ibn Ezra to the go-between (meliz) who carries secrets. Radak, Meiri and Malbim place them as idle men at street corners.

verses.translation_literal: But rather in the Torah of YHWH [is] his delight, and in his Torah he murmurs by day and by night.
verses.translation_dramatic: No — his joy lies elsewhere: in the Torah of the LORD. That is where his heart is set, and over his Torah his lips move low and steady, through the daylight and again through the dark.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the three refusals comes the pivot: kî ’im, "but rather". Radak and Metzudat David both stress the point: to avoid evil is not yet to be blessed; the man has something he is for. The Hebrew is exact, with chephets, "delight, pleasure", the word for what a person truly wants (Radak: it includes study and practice). It is desire, not duty. Play the character as someone who enjoys this.

Torah means "instruction", teaching, not only the legal code and not "law" as a bare rulebook. The KJV's "law" narrows it. The verb יֶהְגֶּה (yehgeh) is the second thing the KJV flattens: "meditate" sounds silent and contemplative, but the root hagah is a low sound, as of a moaning dove or a lion growling over its prey (Isa 31:4, an observation of mine). Metzudat Zion says it can be thought or speech; Rashi reads it as of the heart. In the ancient world one read aloud, mumbling the text. Picture a man murmuring the words to himself as he works.

The repetition torat YHWH ... torato is deliberate: Rashi, Radak and Meiri (citing Avodah Zarah 19a) read the second "his Torah" as the man's own, the teaching that was the LORD's has become his, by labor. The Hebrew allows either subject. "Day and night" (yomam wa-laylah) is a merism for always: Radak adds that on the plain sense it means whenever he is free from earning a living.

philological_notes.note: 'His delight, his pleasure, what he wants'. Radak says it includes both study and doing; Malbim says the man must do the good because it is good and commanded, not for reward.

A low sound: murmuring aloud or musing in the heart. Rashi ties it to the heart (Ps 19:15 'the meditation of my heart'); Metzudat Zion allows both thought and speech (Ps 35:28 'my tongue shall murmur your righteousness'). 'Meditate' in KJV captures only the first.

verses.translation_literal: And he will be like a tree planted upon channels of water, which gives its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither, and all that he does, it succeeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so he will be like a tree — set in the ground by a hand that chose the place — standing beside the watercourses. In its season the fruit comes, never late. Its leaves stay green and do not fade, and whatever he puts his hand to comes through.
verses.directors_commentary:
The simile is more specific than the KJV's "planted by the rivers of water" suggests. A shatul tree is one that has been transplanted, set out on purpose (Malbim draws the distinction from a tree that simply grew where it fell), and palgê mayim are not rivers but channels, small divided streams. Rashi glosses the word with an Old French term for a watercourse; Metzudat Zion says it comes from the verb "to divide", i.e. irrigation ditches cut from a main stream. In a land where rain is seasonal and summer is rainless, this is a tree that never has to wait for the weather: Radak points out that the tree on dry ground fruits late and its leaves wither from dryness.

The opening וְהָיָה (vehayah) is a sequential perfect: the consequence of verses 1-2. Because he refuses that company and delights in the Torah, "so he will be" like this tree; Meiri says the same with "and then he will be" (ואז יהיה). The KJV's "shall be" is a fair rendering and so is the ASV's. It is not a bare description of the present, nor a wish, but a settled result: the sort of thing that is always true of such a man. YLT's "he hath been" is the outlier.

The pronouns slide on purpose. "Its fruit ... its leaf" is the tree; "all that he does" is the man. Ibn Ezra and Radak list the readings of the last clause: the man prospers; or whatever is cut from the tree and replanted takes root (Radak, Metzudat David: his children turn out like him). The Hebrew does not choose, and neither does the literal layer. yatsliach is causative in form ("it causes to succeed / go through") with no stated object, so the line says only that things come out well.

The KJV's "prosper" can sound like material wealth. The Hebrew verb is broader: to push through, to come out right. And in Rashi's reading, "its leaf does not wither" says that even the leftovers of the scholar's talk are worth learning from (Avodah Zarah 19b).

philological_notes.note: Transplanted, deliberately set out. Malbim distinguishes it from נָטוּעַ (planted where it stands). Metzudat Zion glosses 'planted' with Ps 92:14.
Irrigation channels, water divided off from a larger stream; not 'rivers' as in KJV. The root פלג means 'to divide'.
To wither, fade (Isa 1:30 'like an oak whose leaf withers'). Rashi glosses it as 'fading'.

verses.translation_literal: Not so the wicked ones, but rather like chaff which wind drives away.
verses.translation_dramatic: Not so the wicked. They are chaff — the dry husk, light as breath — and when the wind rises it carries them off.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tree had roots, water, time. The chaff has none of these: motz is the husk and broken straw that comes off the grain on a threshing floor, thrown into the air so the wind blows it away while the heavy grain falls (Hos 13:3, cited by Metzudat Zion). The ancient audience knew this image from the harvest: the value is in what stays, and chaff is what is thrown out. Rashi glosses it as straw, Radak as the fine part of the straw, useless as food.

The verse is as short as the previous was long, and has no verb of its own: "not so ... but like". The shortness is the point. The verb tiddefennu is a feminine form agreeing with ruach ("wind", which is feminine in Hebrew). Metzudat Zion links nadaf to being driven or beaten (Lev 26:36, a leaf that is driven). The KJV renders the wind as "driveth away"; the Hebrew picture is a push that does not stop. Note that the wicked here are not struck down by God; they have no weight, so any wind removes them.

Two small points: KJV "ungodly" appears again for רְשָׁעִים; and the "kî ’im" is the same adversative "but rather" as in verse 2, which sets the two men face to face, tree against chaff.

philological_notes.note: Chaff, the husks separated from grain on the threshing floor (Hos 13:3). Rashi says straw; Ibn Ezra says it is the fine part of the straw, lighter than tebben.
To drive, scatter; the first nun of the root has assimilated into the dalet, which gives the doubled 'dd'. Metzudat Zion ties it to being pushed or driven (Lev 26:36 'a driven leaf').

verses.translation_literal: Therefore wicked ones will not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of righteous ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so, when judgment comes, the wicked will not be able to stand. The sinners will have no place in the circle of the righteous.
verses.directors_commentary:
The "therefore" ('al ken) is the hinge of the psalm: because they are chaff, they will not hold. The verb yaqumu means "rise, stand up", in a courtroom the posture of a party who can keep their ground (as in a case that "stands"), so the line says they will not be able to face the verdict. The KJV's "shall not stand" gets this right; BBE's "no mercy" invents a plot that is not in the Hebrew.

The clause "in the judgment" (bammishpat) has the definite article, the judgment, and the commentators cannot settle when. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as a post-mortem accounting; Metzudat David and Meiri as the time when the measure of a life is taken. Keep the actors from playing a specific court; the text does not describe one.

The second half is a compact clause with the verb carried over: "nor [will] sinners [stand] in the ‘edat of the righteous". ‘Edah is the gathered community, the assembly that Israel is called elsewhere; it is the group that holds together. So the contrast with chaff is complete: the wicked scatter, the righteous are assembled. Malbim notes the two terms differ again: the resha‘im fail alone, the hatta’im, who are lighter, might stand alone but not among the righteous.

philological_notes.note: 'Rise, stand up'; of a legal case or a person, to stand firm. Radak reads 'there will be no rising for them' at death.
The assembly, congregation: a gathering by appointment. Ibn Ezra reads the point as 'their company is good for all', the opposite of a band of wicked.

verses.translation_literal: For YHWH knows the way of righteous ones, and the way of wicked ones will perish.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD knows the road the righteous walk. But the road of the wicked — that road runs out, and no one will find where it went.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes by setting the two roads against each other, and with them the two words that opened it: "way" (derekh) in verse 1 now ends the psalm, twice. The verb yode‘a is a participle, a continuing action: the LORD is knowing, always. In Hebrew, to "know" someone is not just to have information but to be attentive and involved. Radak glosses it "recognizes and attends, to do good", Metzudat Zion cites Exodus 2:25 ("and God knew"). The KJV's "knoweth" is accurate but sounds like a fact held in a file; this is closer to watching over.

The last verb, to’ved, is feminine singular and agrees with the second derekh: it is the road that perishes, not first of all the people. Roads are real things in the ancient East: a way that is not walked, not maintained, and not known disappears into the wilderness. So the wicked's path is the path that ends nowhere, and the contrast is between the way the LORD tends and the one he doesn't. Radak and Malbim read this as the loss of the soul's survival, Meiri and Metzudat David as a loss of the LORD's care. The Hebrew says only that it perishes; play it unembellished.

The KJV's "ungodly" returns once more for רְשָׁעִים, the word that began the psalm's list of company in verse 1. The Hebrew repeats resha‘im in verses 1, 4, 5 and 6 and the psalm ends where it began; keep that echo audible.

philological_notes.note: Participle: 'is knowing'. Radak: 'recognizes and watches over for good', citing Ps 144:3 and Exod 3:7. Metzudat Zion: 'providence', as in Exod 2:25.

'Will perish, be lost'; feminine singular, agreeing with 'way'. Radak and Malbim read an end for the souls of the wicked; Meiri and Metzudat David a loss of the LORD's care and of a place among the righteous.
